1198.title: Reading (ch. 48)
1198.howItsDone: Benedictine communities set aside time each day for lectio divina, the slow, prayerful reading of scripture, and some lay Catholics practice it on their own or in parish groups.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ora et labora, and the Rule's blunt line that idleness is the enemy of the soul. Your line was pray and work.

When Lent begins, Saint Benedict's Rule says, each monk is handed a book from the library, and he's to read it straight through, from start to finish. Not skim it. Not sample a chapter and move on. It's the same chapter as yesterday, chapter forty-eight, the one that called idleness the enemy. Yesterday was the work of the hands. But the chapter sets aside other hours, every day, for something just as deliberate.
screen: `IN LENT, A BOOK FROM THE LIBRARY.` → `READ IT STRAIGHT THROUGH.` → `THE OTHER HALF OF CHAPTER 48.`

segments.voice: Benedict's timetable is careful. At certain hours the brothers work with their hands, and at certain hours they're free for holy reading. The hours shift with the seasons, but the reading is always there, set into the day like the prayers. This is what Catholics call lectio divina, holy reading, which you walked through step by step back around day two hundred thirty-three. It isn't reading for information, racing to the end. It's slow: read scripture or a holy book, stop when a line catches, turn it over, let it sink, and maybe turn it into prayer. The first psalm describes a person like that, in the Douay-Rheims: "on his law he shall meditate day and night." Benedict knows reading time can go soft. So during the reading hours, one or two senior monks go around the monastery to make sure no brother is idle or chatting, bothering others instead of reading. On Sunday, everyone is free for reading, except those with duties to do. And if a brother is so careless that he can't or won't read, he's given some work, so he isn't idle. Even then, the answer is something useful, never nothing. What's striking is the respect the Rule gives to reading. It isn't a hobby for the scholarly monks. It's a daily duty for everyone, at fixed hours, like prayer and work. The hope behind it is that a few lines read slowly, day after day, can reshape a person, the way water shapes a stone.

segments.voice: Choose what you'd read slowly, a Gospel passage, a psalm, a page of a saint, or any book that feeds you, and when and where: a set hour, a chair, a corner, phone in another room. Picture yourself reading one line, stopping, and reading it again, with no rush to the end of the page. If you pray, let the line you stop on become your prayer.

1199.title: Guests as Christ (ch. 53)
1199.hook: let all guests be received as Christ
1199.howItsDone: Benedictine monasteries keep guesthouses and receive retreatants and visitors, and Catholics often point to chapter fifty-three and Matthew 25 when they talk about hospitality.

segments.voice: Yesterday, reading: holy reading at set hours, slow enough to stop on a single line. Your line was hours for reading.

A knock at the monastery gate, late, after supper. Dusty boots, a pack, a stranger nobody was expecting. Inside, the monks are just settling into quiet after a long day, and an unplanned visitor at the wrong hour can make a whole house sigh. Saint Benedict's Rule doesn't pretend the knock is convenient. But chapter fifty-three tells the monks exactly who is standing at the gate, and it isn't just a stranger.
screen: `A KNOCK, LATE, AFTER SUPPER.` → `NOBODY WAS EXPECTING HIM.` → `WHO IS AT THE GATE?`

segments.voice: The chapter opens: let all guests who come be received as Christ. Benedict gives the reason in Christ's own words from Matthew, in the Douay-Rheims: "I was a stranger, and you took me in." So the guest isn't an interruption to the monks' life with God. Some readers put it this way: the guest is that life arriving in person. Then Benedict turns it into a ceremony. The superior and the brothers go out to meet the guest with every mark of love. They pray together first, and only then exchange the kiss of peace. They bow their heads, or even lie down on the ground, honoring Christ, who is received in the guest. The abbot pours water over the guest's hands, and the abbot and the whole community wash the guest's feet. Then a line that's easy to read past. Benedict asks for the greatest care for the poor and for pilgrims, because in them, he says, Christ is received more. The rich, he notes dryly, get honored anyway; people are in awe of them. The poor depend on the welcome. Benedict is practical, too. The abbot and guests get their own kitchen, so guests turning up at odd hours, and he says guests never stop turning up, don't throw the brothers' day into chaos. A sensible brother is put in charge of the guest house. Nobody has to choose between keeping the house running and opening the door. The door opens because the house is ordered.

1200.title: Tools as altar vessels (ch. 31)
1200.hook: the cellarer treats every tool as a sacred vessel of the altar
1200.howItsDone: Benedictine communities appoint a cellarer to manage the monastery's goods, and Benedictine writers sometimes point to the Rule's line about treating every tool like an altar vessel when they speak about care for ordinary things.

segments.voice: Yesterday, guests as Christ: the knock at the gate, the washed feet, the greatest care for the poor. Your line was received as Christ.

Two objects on a table. One is a chalice, the cup the priest lifts at Mass, polished, kept in a safe place, handled with care. The other is a dented saucepan from a monastery kitchen, with a burnt spot on the bottom. Nobody would mix them up. One is sacred and one is a pan. Saint Benedict's Rule mixes them up on purpose: in chapter thirty-one, about the monk who runs the storerooms, the saucepan is to be treated like the chalice.
screen: `A CHALICE AND A SAUCEPAN.` → `ONE SACRED, ONE A PAN?` → `THE RULE MIXES THEM UP.`

segments.voice: The monk in charge is called the cellarer. He keeps the stores: food, tools, cloth, everything the house runs on. Benedict's description of him reads like a character sketch. He should be wise, mature, sober, not a big eater, not proud, not stormy, not unkind, not slow, not wasteful, someone who fears God and is like a father to the whole community. Then the line the day is named for. He is to look upon all the vessels and goods of the monastery as if they were the consecrated vessels of the altar, and neglect nothing. The rake, the ladle, the sack of grain: handled with the care the priest gives the chalice. Why? One way to read it: in his monastery, no part of life sits outside God. Paul says it in the Douay-Rheims: "whether you eat or drink, or whatsoever else you do, do all to the glory of God." Then the pot that cooks the brothers' soup serves God too, and carelessness with it isn't just untidiness; it's a small failure of reverence. The chapter doesn't stop at things. The cellarer is told not to make the brothers sad. If someone asks for something unreasonable, he refuses gently and gives a reason, not a brush-off. If he has nothing to give, he gives a kind word. He cares for the sick, the children, the guests and the poor with every attention. The reverence that keeps the ladle clean keeps a brother from feeling dismissed. Things and people, handled as holy.

1201.title: The sick first (ch. 36)
1201.hook: care of the sick is placed above all
1201.howItsDone: Benedictine communities care for their sick and elderly members within the monastery, and Catholics count visiting the sick among the corporal works of mercy drawn from Matthew 25.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tools as altar vessels: the saucepan handled like the chalice. Your line was everything is holy.

Before all things, and above all things. Strong words for any rule to use, and Saint Benedict doesn't spend them lightly. Earlier this week the Rule said nothing is to be put before the work of God. So what could come before all things? Not the abbot. Not the chapel. Not the harvest or the library. Chapter thirty-six answers in its first line, and the answer is the brother lying in the infirmary with a fever.
screen: `BEFORE ALL THINGS, ABOVE ALL THINGS.` → `WHAT COULD COME BEFORE EVERYTHING?` → `THE BROTHER WITH A FEVER.`

segments.voice: Benedict writes that care of the sick must come before all things and above all things, so that they are served as Christ himself. He gives Christ's words from Matthew, in the Douay-Rheims: "sick, and you visited me," and "as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me." One way to hold the two "before" lines together: the work of God comes first, and the sick are served as Christ. The same Christ, in the chapel and in the sickbed. Then Benedict gets specific. The sick get their own room, and a brother to look after them who is God-fearing, careful and attentive. They may have baths as often as it helps them. The very weak may eat meat, normally kept off the monks' table, to get their strength back; when they recover, they go back to the usual fare. The abbot takes the greatest care that the sick suffer no neglect, and checks that the cellarer and attendants let nothing slip. Here's the part that keeps it honest. Benedict speaks to the sick, too. They should remember they're served for the honor of God, and not wear out their brothers with unreasonable demands. Then, in the very next breath, he tells the brothers: bear with them patiently anyway, because from such as these a greater reward is gained. Patience is asked of both sides of the bed. Nobody in this chapter is a saint already. They're just people being asked to carry each other.

1202.title: Three vows (ch. 58)
1202.howItsDone: Benedictine monks and nuns make their vows of stability, conversion of life and obedience during Mass or in the community's church, and the written promise is placed on the altar, as the Rule describes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sick first: in Benedict's Rule, care of the sick comes before all things, because they are served as Christ. Your line was before all things.

Don't make it easy to get in. That's roughly how chapter fifty-eight of Saint Benedict's Rule greets newcomers who ask to join. The one who asks is left waiting, and has to put up with a little rudeness at the door, to see if he means it. If he keeps asking, he's let in, first to the guest house, then to the novices. The Rule itself is read aloud to him, more than once: this is the law you want to serve under. If you can keep it, come in. If not, you are free to go. Today, the promise he makes at the end of all that.
screen: `ENTRY NOT MADE EASY.` → `THE RULE READ TO HIM, AGAIN.` → `IF YOU CAN KEEP IT, COME IN.`

segments.voice: When the time comes, the novice stands before the whole community in the oratory, the place of prayer, and promises three things: stability, conversion of life, and obedience. Obedience had its own day earlier. Today is the first one, stability: binding yourself to one community, in one place, for life. A monk doesn't go looking for a better monastery when this one gets hard. He stays with these brothers, this abbot, this kitchen, this choir. In the Rule's first chapter, Benedict has sharp words for monks who wander from house to house. Stability is his answer to that restlessness. Conversion of life is harder to pin down. The Latin phrase is unusual, and readers argue over its exact sense. Some hear a promise to live the monastic way of life; others, a promise to keep being changed, day after day. The novice writes his promise out, in his own hand if he can, and lays it on the altar himself. He sings a verse from the psalms, in the Douay-Rheims: "Uphold me according to thy word, and I shall live: and let me not be confounded in my expectation." The community sings it back to him. Then he lies at each brother's feet and asks for their prayers, and from that day, the Rule says, he's counted one of them. The first vow isn't about doing anything grand. It's about not leaving. The holiness Benedict has in mind grows in one patch of ground, among the same faces.

1203.title: Good zeal (ch. 72)
1203.hook: bear one another's weaknesses of body and character with patience
1203.howItsDone: Benedictine communities read the Rule aloud in portions through the year, and chapter seventy-two on good zeal is often cited by monks and oblates as a summary of how to live together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, stability: the monk's promise to stay with one community, in one place, for life. Your line was stay.

Zeal has a mixed reputation. A zealous fan, a zealous inspector, a zealous neighbor with a clipboard and opinions about your lawn. Fire, yes, but often the kind that burns other people. Near the very end of his Rule, after chapters on prayer, work, food, sleep and punishment, Benedict stops to talk about zeal. He doesn't tell his monks to have less of it. He says there are two kinds, and they lead in opposite directions. Today: good zeal.
screen: `ZEAL: FIRE THAT CAN BURN.` → `NEAR THE END OF THE RULE.` → `TWO KINDS, TWO DIRECTIONS.`

segments.voice: Chapter seventy-two is short, and it opens with the contrast. There is a bad zeal of bitterness, Benedict says, which separates a person from God and leads toward hell. And there is a good zeal, which separates a person from vices and leads toward God and everlasting life. Same energy, opposite ends. The bitter kind keeps a list of everyone else's faults. The good kind is what monks should practice with the warmest love, and his list of what it looks like is almost all about other people. First, outdo one another in showing honor. That echoes Saint Paul in the Douay-Rheims: "Loving one another with the charity of brotherhood, with honour preventing one another." Preventing is an old sense: going ahead, getting there first. Then the line today is built on: bear one another's weaknesses, of body or of character, with the greatest patience. Of body: the brother who snores, who's slow, who's sick again. Of character: the one who interrupts, who sulks, who is exactly as irritating today as yesterday. Benedict doesn't say fix them or report them. He says bear them. Paul again: "Bear ye one another's burdens; and so you shall fulfil the law of Christ." No one should chase what seems best for himself, but what is best for someone else. And the chapter ends: prefer nothing whatever to Christ, and may he bring us all together to everlasting life. Benedict's last picture of heaven includes the snorer.

Good zeal. In Benedict's Rule, the fire that leads away from vice and toward God, and shows itself in honor and patience toward others. Today's word.
Your line: bear with each other. Good zeal shows itself as honor and patience. Go gently.

1204.title: A little rule (ch. 73)
1204.hook: Benedict calls it a little rule for beginners
1204.howItsDone: Benedictines speak of the monastic life as a lifelong beginning, and the Rule, ending with this chapter, is read through again from the Prologue in houses that read it in a cycle.

segments.voice: Yesterday, good zeal: honor others first, and carry their weaknesses with patience. Your line was bear with each other.

A man writes out a rule for a whole way of life. Prayer through the day and night, work, food, sleep, the sick, the guests, the tools, the vows, what to do when someone is late for dinner. Then he reaches the final page. A reader might expect a flourish: this is the complete path, follow it and you'll arrive. Benedict writes something close to the opposite. He calls the whole thing a little rule, written for beginners. Today, the Rule's closing chapter.
screen: `A WHOLE WAY OF LIFE, WRITTEN DOWN.` → `THE FINAL PAGE.` → `A LITTLE RULE, FOR BEGINNERS.`

segments.voice: Chapter seventy-three opens with an admission. Benedict wrote this Rule, he says, so that by keeping it, monks might show some measure of good living and a beginning of the monastic life. A beginning, not a finish line. For anyone hurrying on toward something more, there are better teachers. Then he points away from himself. First to Scripture: what page, what word of the Old and New Testaments, he asks, is not a true guide for human life? Then to the writers before him: the holy fathers, the Conferences and Institutes of John Cassian, the lives of the desert monks, the rule of Saint Basil. Next to those, his own work is small. And the last sentence, to whoever is reading: if you are hurrying toward your heavenly home, keep, with Christ's help, this little rule for beginners, and then, under God's protection, you will reach the greater heights he has just named. These past days brought hours for reading, guests received as Christ, kitchen tools treated like vessels of the altar, the sick put first, a promise to stay, the patience to bear each other. All of that, Benedict calls a start. The humility of the ladder chapter turns out to be the author's own. And the beginner isn't someone who will soon stop being one. In the Prologue, Benedict called his monastery a school. Here at the end, he's still enrolling students.
screen: `A BEGINNING, NOT A FINISH LINE.` · `HE POINTS TO SCRIPTURE AND THE FATHERS.` · `THESE PAST DAYS, CALLED A START.` · then, large: `THIS LITTLE RULE FOR BEGINNERS.` · then: `STILL ENROLLING STUDENTS.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing from these chapters you meant to try and didn't, or tried once and dropped: the hour of reading, the guest, the patience. Don't grade yourself; pick it up again now, the way a beginner picks up a pencil on the first day of school, and breathe out the last attempt. If you pray, borrow a psalm line from the Douay-Rheims: "Now have I begun."
A little rule. Benedict's own name for his Rule in its closing chapter: a small rule, written for beginners, pointing beyond itself to Scripture and the fathers. Today's word.
Your line: always beginning. For Benedict, even the whole Rule was only a start. Until tomorrow.
